body.heading: Move chairs, literally in your mind
paragraphs: Pick the person you are puzzled by and imagine their day from the inside: their commute, their worries, the last three things that happened before they met you. Behaviour that looks rude from your chair often looks like coping from theirs.
This is not about agreeing with them. It is about making their actions legible before you decide what to do.

body.heading: List what they might be protecting
paragraphs: Most sharp reactions protect something: pride, time, money, a child, a reputation, a fragile hope. Ask yourself what this person might be afraid of losing. The answer usually softens your interpretation, even when the behaviour still needs addressing.
A manager who snaps about a deadline may be protecting their own standing. A friend who cancels may be protecting the last of their energy.

body.heading: Check your story before you use it
paragraphs: Your imagined version of their view is a draft, not a fact. If it matters, test it with one humble question: “I might have this wrong, but are you worried about…?” Being corrected is not failure; it is the method working.
Perspective-taking that never gets checked is just storytelling. The checking is what turns it into understanding.

takeaway: Imagine their day, guess what they are protecting, and check your story before you trust it.
